title: Stoichiometry, Limiting Reagent Protocol & Reaction Yields

conceptBreakdown.heading: 7. The Stoichiometric Conversion Bridge
conceptBreakdown.title: 7. The Stoichiometric Conversion Bridge

summaryBox.title: Stoichiometry Conversion Path
summaryBox.takeaway: Mass A (g) → Moles A (n_A = w_A / M_A) → Moles B (n_B = n_A · b/a) → Mass B (w_B = n_B · M_B).

conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
STOICHIOMETRIC CONVERSION BRIDGE
                      
   Mass Reactant A (g) ──► Moles A ($n_A = w_A/M_A$) ──► Moles B ($n_B = n_A \cdot \frac{b}{a}$) ──► Mass B ($w_B = n_B M_B$)
conceptBreakdown.content:
For a balanced chemical equation: $a A + b B \longrightarrow c C + d D$

Stoichiometry connects quantities through molar relationships. Always convert given reactant quantities into moles before applying stoichiometric coefficients.

conceptBreakdown.heading: 7.1 The Limiting Reagent (LR) Protocol
conceptBreakdown.title: 7.1 The Limiting Reagent (LR) Protocol
conceptBreakdown.content:
The Limiting Reagent is the reactant completely consumed first, placing an absolute upper bound on product yield.

**3-Step Protocol**:
1. Calculate initial moles available for each reactant ($n_A$ and $n_B$).
2. Divide moles by balanced stoichiometric coefficients: $\frac{n_A}{a}$ and $\frac{n_B}{b}$.
3. Compare:
   • If $\frac{n_A}{a} < \frac{n_B}{b} \implies \mathbf{A\text{ is the Limiting Reagent (LR)}}$.
   • If $\frac{n_B}{b} < \frac{n_A}{a} \implies \mathbf{B\text{ is the Limiting Reagent (LR)}}$.
   • If $\frac{n_A}{a} = \frac{n_B}{b} \implies \text{Stoichiometric proportion (both consumed completely)}.$

conceptBreakdown.heading: 7.2 Reaction Yields & Sample Purity
conceptBreakdown.title: 7.2 Reaction Yields & Sample Purity
conceptBreakdown.content:
• **Percentage Yield**:
$$\mathbf{\% \text{ Yield} = \frac{\text{Actual Experimental Yield}}{\text{Theoretical Calculated Yield}} \times 100}$$

• **Percentage Purity**:
$$\mathbf{\% \text{ Purity} = \frac{\text{Mass of Pure Reactive Component}}{\text{Total Mass of Impure Sample}} \times 100}$$

quickRevision: Limiting reagent is identified by min(n_initial / coefficient).
Theoretical yield is calculated strictly from the limiting reagent.
